verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(A): the plaintiff 'shall contemporaneously file a Notice of Intent to File Suit and an affidavit of an expert witness, subject to the affidavit requirements established in Section 15-36-100, in a county in which venue would be proper'; the notice 'must name all adverse parties as defendants' and 'must be served upon all named defendants in accordance with the service rules for a summons and complaint'.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim 2026-10-02.

verifiedClaims.claim: Include an affidavit of an expert witness who has reviewed the medical records and identified at least one negligent act and the resulting damages
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The affidavit 'must specify at least one negligent act or omission claimed to exist and the factual basis for each claim based on the available evidence at the time of the filing of the affidavit' (§ 15-36-100(B), incorporated by § 15-79-125(A)). The statute does not require the affidavit to identify 'the resulting damages'.
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: 'Include an affidavit of an expert witness that specifies at least one negligent act or omission and the factual basis for it (S.C. Code § 15-36-100)'. Same correction in faq:5.

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing the notice tolls the statute of limitations, and the parties must then mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, before the lawsuit can be filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 'Filing the Notice of Intent to File Suit tolls all applicable statutes of limitations' (§ 15-79-125(A)). 'Within ninety days and no later than one hundred twenty days from the service of the Notice of Intent to File Suit, the parties shall participate in a mediation conference unless an extension for no more than sixty days is granted by the court based upon a finding of good cause' (§ 15-79-125(C)). If mediation fails, suit must be filed within 60 days of the mediator's impasse declaration or before the limitation period expires, whichever is later ((E), facts-1696).
verifiedClaims.note: 'Generally' covers the 60-day good-cause extension.

verifiedClaims.claim: The expert affidavit must be from a qualified medical professional — not just any expert — who practices or has recently practiced in the same specialty as the defendant.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(A): the expert must be 'qualified as to the acceptable conduct of the professional whose conduct is at issue', licensed 'to practice his or her profession', and EITHER (2)(a) board certified in the area of practice or specialty about which the opinion is offered, OR (2)(b) regularly engaged in active practice, teaching, or a combination in that area 'for at least three of the last five years immediately preceding the opinion'; OR (3) an individual with 'scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge which may assist the trier of fact', whose affidavit must explain the expert's credentials and why the expert is qualified.
verifiedClaims.note: Board certification is an independent route, and (A)(3) is a further catch-all, so 'practices or has recently practiced in the same specialty' overstates it. Minimal edit: 'The expert must be qualified in the defendant's area of practice — board certified in it, or actively practicing or teaching in it for at least three of the last five years (S.C. Code § 15-36-100).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Failure to comply with the notice requirement can result in dismissal of your case.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: No affidavit: 'the complaint is subject to dismissal for failure to state a claim' on a motion filed with the defendant's initial responsive pleading (§ 15-36-100(C)(1)); a defective affidavit may be cured 'by amendment within thirty days of service of the motion' ((E)).
verifiedClaims.note: 'Can result' is accurate. Optional add: a defective affidavit can be cured by amendment within 30 days of the motion.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina law (S.C. Code § 15-36-100) establishes strict qualifications for expert witnesses in medical malpractice cases:
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(A) applies to professional negligence generally (the professions listed in (G)), and its three alternative routes include (A)(3), a person with 'scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge' — so the qualifications are specific, not 'strict'. The (C)(2) common-knowledge exception dispenses with the affidavit for negligence 'within the ambit of common knowledge and experience'.

verifiedClaims.currentValue: 'The provisions of this section do not limit the amount of compensation for economic damages suffered by each claimant in a medical malpractice claim' (§ 15-32-220(D)(1)).

Also, the limit against all health care providers and all health care institutions for each claimant ... increases to $1,788,002. The adjusted limitations ... become effective upon publication in the State Register' (§ 15-32-220(F)).

verifiedClaims.claim: Subject to that cap, you can recover:
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Only noneconomic damages are subject to the cap: economic damages (§ 15-32-220(D)(1)) and punitive damages ((D)(2)) are not. And the cap does not apply at all 'if the jury or court determines that the defendant was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton, or reckless, and such conduct was the proximate cause of the claimant's noneconomic damages, or if the defendant has engaged in fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or if the defendant altered or destroyed medical records with the purpose of avoiding a claim or liability' (§ 15-32-220(E)). Intoxication is NOT a § 15-32-220 exception (it lifts the punitive cap under § 15-32-530(C)(3)).

Replace with: 'The cap does not apply if the provider was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, committed fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or altered or destroyed medical records to avoid liability (S.C. verifiedClaims.claim: Punitive damages — awarded only in rare cases and must be proved by clear and convincing evidence (S.C. Code § 15-33-135); South Carolina caps punitive damages at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure (S.C. Code § 15-32-530), with exceptions for certain egregious conduct
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-33-135: 'In any civil action where punitive damages are claimed, the plaintiff has the burden of proving such damages by clear and convincing evidence.' § 15-32-520(D): punitive damages only on clear and convincing proof of 'wilful, wanton, or reckless conduct'; bifurcated trial on any defendant's request (§ 15-32-520(A)). § 15-32-530(A): greater of three times compensatory or $500,000, indexed (D) — RFA memo 2026-02-03: 'the limit increases to $739,245'. Exceptions: four times or $2,000,000 for conduct motivated primarily by unreasonable financial gain known to management, or that could be a felony ((B)); no cap for intent to harm, a felony plea/conviction, or substantial impairment by alcohol or drugs ((C)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code §§ 15-33-135, 15-32-520, 15-32-530; RFA memo 'Punitive Damage Award Limitation – Inflation Component', 2026-02-03
verifiedClaims.note: All figures verified. 'Awarded only in rare cases' is characterisation; acceptable. Optional: add 'and requires wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (S.C. Code § 15-32-520)'. Statute text: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c033.php and https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t15c032.php.

verifiedClaims.claim: In many medical malpractice cases, both the individual doctor and the hospital may be liable:
verifiedClaims.currentValue: MUSC's hospitals are run by the Medical University Hospital Authority, 'an agency of the State of South Carolina' (S.C. Code § 59-123-60(E)); 'MUSC is a governmental agency subject to the provisions of the Tort Claims Act' (Tatum v. Medical University of South Carolina, 346 S.C. 194 (2001), citing Proveaux v. MUSC, 326 S.C. 28 (1997)). Consequences: (1) the Act 'constitutes the exclusive remedy for any tort committed by an employee of a governmental entity' and an employee acting within the scope of official duty 'is not liable therefor' (§ 15-78-70(a)); the plaintiff 'shall name as a party defendant only the agency' (§ 15-78-70(c)) — so a salaried MUSC physician (including one paid through an MUSC practice plan) is generally not a separate defendant (Tatum; § 15-78-70(c) proviso); (2) suit is 'forever barred unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered', three years if a verified claim was first filed (§ 15-78-110); (3) recovery is capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120(a)(1)-(2)), but where the loss is 'caused by the tort of any licensed physician or dentist, employed by a governmental entity', the per-person and per-occurrence limit is $1,200,000 (§ 15-78-120(a)(3)-(4)); (4) 'No award for damages under this chapter shall include punitive or exemplary damages or interest prior to judgment' (§ 15-78-120(b)). Definitions expressly include 'state-supported governmental health care facilit[ies]' (§ 15-78-30(a),(e)).
verifiedClaims.note: Major omission for a Charleston hospital post that names MUSC four times: a claim against MUSC (or another public hospital) runs under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, not ordinary rules. Add a bullet: 'Public hospitals — MUSC is a state agency, so a claim against it falls under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act: you generally sue MUSC rather than its employed doctors, suit must be filed within two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), damages are capped (generally $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence, or $1.2 million where an MUSC-employed physician or dentist was negligent — S.C. Code § 15-78-120), and punitive damages are not available.' The § 15-79-125 Notice of Intent still applies to med-mal claims. Tatum: https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1285904/tatum-v-medical-university-of-south-carolina/ ; § 59-123-60: https://www.scstatehouse.gov/code/t59c123.php. Whether § 15-78-110's two years displaces § 15-3-545's three years for a med-mal claim against MUSC is the statute's plain text ('any action brought pursuant to this chapter'); attorney should confirm the phrasing.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hospital liability — hospitals are liable for the negligence of their employees (nurses, technicians, employed physicians) under respondeat superior.
verifiedClaims.note: General rule accurate for private hospitals (Roper St. Francis, Trident, Novant East Cooper). For MUSC the hospital is liable but its employees are immune and must not be named (§ 15-78-70) — covered by the new bullet above.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hospitals may also be directly liable for understaffing, inadequate training, equipment failures, and systemic failures in safety protocols
verifiedClaims.note: General direct-negligence statement; no South Carolina corporate-negligence case was verified this run — do not add a case citation for it.

verifiedClaims.claim: However, if the hospital holds the doctor out as its agent (such as ER physicians who wear hospital badges), the hospital may still be liable under the doctrine of apparent or ostensible agency
verifiedClaims.currentValue: For emergency rooms South Carolina goes further than apparent agency. Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center, 341 S.C. 32, 533 S.E.2d 312 (2000): 'a hospital owes a nondelegable duty to render competent service to its emergency room patients', adopting Restatement (Second) of Torts § 429: the plaintiff must show '(1) the hospital held itself out to the public by offering to provide services; (2) the plaintiff looked to the hospital, rather than the individual physician, for care; and (3) a person in similar circumstances reasonably would have believed that the physician who treated him or her was a hospital employee', and the hospital 'will be held vicariously liable for any negligent or wrongful acts committed by the treating physician'. The holding 'is not necessarily limited to' ER physicians but does not cover a patient's own physician met at the ER. Traditional apparent agency (representation, reliance, detrimental change of position) remains available; the court noted hospitals cannot escape by 'last-minute notice ... through admission forms or emergency room signs'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center, 341 S.C. 32, 533 S.E.2d 312 (S.C. 2000) (CourtListener)
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: '...the hospital may still be liable. For emergency-room physicians, South Carolina imposes a nondelegable duty on the hospital (Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center, 2000): if the hospital offered the services, you looked to the hospital for care, and a reasonable person would have believed the doctor was a hospital employee, the hospital is liable for the doctor's negligence — even if a consent form called the doctor an independent contractor.' Justia copy (403 to curl): https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2000/25143.html

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina medical malpractice claims require a pre-suit Notice of Intent to File and an expert witness affidavit establishing the standard of care was breached.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-79-125(A): 'Notice of Intent to File Suit' filed contemporaneously with an expert affidavit that 'must specify at least one negligent act or omission claimed to exist and the factual basis for each claim' (§ 15-36-100(B)).
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: '...a pre-suit Notice of Intent to File Suit, filed with an expert affidavit identifying at least one negligent act or omission, followed by mandatory mediation.'

verifiedClaims.claim: The statute of limitations is 3 years with a 6-year statute of repose.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-545(A) three years / six-year repose verified; but claims against MUSC or another public hospital have a two-year Tort Claims Act deadline (§ 15-78-110).
verifiedClaims.note: Add: '(2 years under the Tort Claims Act if the hospital is MUSC or another public hospital).' The box renders above the article.

verifiedClaims.claim: Hospitals may be liable for employee physician negligence but may argue independent contractor status for affiliated doctors.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Simmons v. Tuomey, 341 S.C. 32 (2000): hospitals owe a nondelegable duty to ER patients; a hospital that held itself out as providing the services is liable for a contractor physician the patient reasonably believed was a hospital employee.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center (S.C. 2000)
verifiedClaims.note: As written the takeaway implies the independent-contractor defense works. Minimal edit: '...may argue independent contractor status for affiliated doctors — but South Carolina holds hospitals liable for emergency-room physicians who appear to be hospital staff (Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center, 2000).'

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia allows 2 years to file (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) and requires an expert affidavit.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified in facts-1696.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina caps non-economic damages at $596,001 per provider or institution and $1,788,002 in total for 2026 (S.C. Code § 15-32-220).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: RFA memo 2026-02-03 verified. Cap lifted under § 15-32-220(E) (gross negligence, wilful/wanton/reckless conduct, fraud, altered/destroyed records).
verifiedClaims.note: Figures correct. Optional add: 'per patient; the cap does not apply to gross negligence or reckless conduct'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider fails to provide care that meets the accepted standard of care in their specialty, and that failure causes injury to the patient.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Remainder of answer (four elements; bad outcome alone not malpractice) accurate.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. South Carolina requires an expert affidavit from a qualified medical professional filed together with the Notice of Intent to File Suit (S.C. Code section 15-79-125).
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate. § 15-36-100(C)(2) excuses the affidavit for negligence within common knowledge (rare in hospital cases) — 'Yes' is fine as a general answer.

verifiedClaims.claim: The expert must be licensed and either board certified in the relevant specialty or have practiced or taught in it for at least three of the last five years immediately preceding the opinion (S.C. Code section 15-36-100).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(A)(1)-(2) verbatim; (A)(3) specialized-knowledge route exists as a further alternative.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate statement of the main routes. Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: The statute of limitations is three years from the date of injury or discovery (S.C. Code section 15-3-545).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-545(A): three years 'from the date of the treatment, omission, or operation' or 'from date of discovery or when it reasonably ought to have been discovered'. MUSC/public hospitals: two years (§ 15-78-110).
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: 'The statute of limitations is three years from the date of the treatment, or from when the injury was or reasonably should have been discovered (S.C. Code section 15-3-545) — two years if the hospital is MUSC or another public hospital (S.C. Code section 15-78-110).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Filing the required Notice of Intent to File Suit tolls that deadline (S.C. Code section 15-79-125), but the notice must be filed with an expert's affidavit, so preparation has to start well before it.
South Carolina also has a six-year statute of repose that generally bars claims more than six years after the alleged malpractice regardless of when the injury is discovered.
verifiedClaims.note: 'Generally' covers foreign objects.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina does not cap economic damages in medical malpractice cases, but non-economic damages are capped by S.C. Code § 15-32-220 — a base of $350,000 against a single provider and $1.05 million where more than one is liable, adjusted annually for inflation, so for 2026 the limits are $596,001 and $1,788,002.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Figures verified (§ 15-32-220(A)-(D),(F); RFA memo 2026-02-03). Omitted: the cap does not apply where the defendant was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, committed fraud or misrepresentation related to the claim, or altered or destroyed medical records (§ 15-32-220(E)); claims against MUSC/public hospitals are instead capped by the Tort Claims Act at $300,000 per person / $600,000 per occurrence, or $1.2 million where a government-employed physician or dentist was negligent, with no punitive damages (§ 15-78-120).
verifiedClaims.note: Append: 'The cap does not apply if the provider was grossly negligent, wilful, wanton or reckless, or altered records to avoid liability. Claims against MUSC or another public hospital fall under the Tort Claims Act, which caps damages at $300,000 per person ($1.2 million where an employed physician was negligent) and bars punitive damages (S.C. Code section 15-78-120).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Punitive damages are capped at the greater of three times compensatory damages or $739,245, the 2026 inflation-indexed figure (S.C. Code section 15-32-530), with exceptions for certain egregious conduct.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Hospitals are liable for their employees' negligence under respondeat superior.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: MUSC's hospitals are run by the Medical University Hospital Authority, 'an agency of the State of South Carolina' (S.C. Code § 59-123-60(E)); 'MUSC is a governmental agency subject to the provisions of the Tort Claims Act' (Tatum v. Medical University of South Carolina, 346 S.C. 194 (2001), citing Proveaux v. MUSC, 326 S.C. 28 (1997)). Consequences: (1) the Act 'constitutes the exclusive remedy for any tort committed by an employee of a governmental entity' and an employee acting within the scope of official duty 'is not liable therefor' (§ 15-78-70(a)); the plaintiff 'shall name as a party defendant only the agency' (§ 15-78-70(c)) — so a salaried MUSC physician (including one paid through an MUSC practice plan) is generally not a separate defendant (Tatum; § 15-78-70(c) proviso); (2) suit is 'forever barred unless an action is commenced within two years after the date the loss was or should have been discovered', three years if a verified claim was first filed (§ 15-78-110); (3) recovery is capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (§ 15-78-120(a)(1)-(2)), but where the loss is 'caused by the tort of any licensed physician or dentist, employed by a governmental entity', the per-person and per-occurrence limit is $1,200,000 (§ 15-78-120(a)(3)-(4)); (4) 'No award for damages under this chapter shall include punitive or exemplary damages or interest prior to judgment' (§ 15-78-120(b)). Definitions expressly include 'state-supported governmental health care facilit[ies]' (§ 15-78-30(a),(e)).
verifiedClaims.note: For MUSC (the largest Charleston hospital) the answer to 'can I sue both the hospital and the doctor' is generally no: its employed physicians are immune and MUSC is the only defendant (§ 15-78-70). Add: 'If the hospital is MUSC or another public hospital, the claim runs under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act: you sue the hospital rather than its employed doctors, within two years, and damages are capped (S.C. Code sections 15-78-70, 15-78-110, 15-78-120).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Even if a doctor is technically an independent contractor, the hospital may be liable under apparent agency if it holds the doctor out as its agent.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Simmons v. Tuomey, 341 S.C. 32 (2000): for ER physicians South Carolina imposes a nondelegable duty (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 429) — hospital liable where it offered the services, the patient looked to the hospital, and a reasonable person would have believed the physician was a hospital employee.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center (S.C. 2000)
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: '...if it holds the doctor out as its agent; for emergency-room doctors, South Carolina treats the hospital's duty as nondelegable (Simmons v. Tuomey Regional Medical Center, 2000).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Before filing a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina, you must file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with an expert affidavit, serve it on each defendant, and mediate, generally within 90 to 120 days of service, before filing the complaint (S.C. Code section 15-79-125).
verifiedClaims.note: Verified.

verifiedClaims.claim: The affidavit must come from a qualified medical professional who has reviewed the records and identified at least one negligent act and the resulting damages.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-36-100(B): affidavit 'must specify at least one negligent act or omission claimed to exist and the factual basis for each claim'. No damages element.
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: 'The affidavit must come from a qualified expert and must specify at least one negligent act or omission and the factual basis for it (S.C. Code section 15-36-100).' Publishes as FAQPage structured data.

verifiedClaims.claim: Failure to comply can result in dismissal.

statuteCitations.name: Medical malpractice — three years from treatment or (constructive) discovery, six-year repose (A); foreign objects (B); minors' tolling capped at seven years / one year after majority (D)
Notice of Intent to File Suit with expert affidavit; filing tolls limitations (A); mediation 90–120 days from service, 60-day good-cause extension (C); suit within 60 days of impasse (E)

Expert definition — licensed in own profession; board certified OR 3 of last 5 years practice/teaching; or specialized knowledge (A); affidavit specifying at least one negligent act or omission and factual basis (B); dismissal (C)(1); common-knowledge exception (C)(2); 30-day cure (E)

Med-mal noneconomic cap — $350,000 / $1,050,000 base per claimant (A)-(C); economic and punitive not capped (D); no cap for gross negligence, wilful/wanton/reckless conduct, fraud, altered/destroyed records (E); CPI indexing (F) — $596,001 / $1,788,002 for 2026
Emergency/obstetrical care — physician liable only for gross negligence while patient unstable
Punitive damages — bifurcation on request (A); clear and convincing proof of wilful, wanton or reckless conduct (D)
Punitive cap — greater of 3x compensatory or $500,000 (A), indexed ($739,245 for 2026) (D); 4x / $2,000,000 tier (B); no cap for intent to harm, felony, substantial impairment (C)
Punitive damages — burden of proof clear and convincing evidence

Tort Claims Act — state-supported health care facilities included (30); exclusive remedy, employee immune, name the agency (70); two years from discovery, three if verified claim filed (110); $300,000 / $600,000 caps, $1,200,000 for government-employed physician/dentist torts, no punitive damages (120)
Medical University Hospital Authority — 'an agency of the State of South Carolina'
Georgia med-mal — two years from injury (a); five-year repose (b)
Georgia minors — under five: two years from fifth birthday, repose at tenth birthday
Georgia expert affidavit with complaint (a); 45-day window (b); 30-day cure (e)
Georgia apportionment — barred at 50 percent or more fault (g)
